l: Town Hall of the people of Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Town Hall stands within Altis near the outlet beyond the gymnasium. It contains a hearth with a continually burning fire, an altar of Pan, and a banqueting-hall where victors at Olympia are entertained.

l: people of Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: The people of Elis sacrifice monthly at the altars, using frankincense, honey cakes, olive branches, and libations. They also pour libations to the god of Libya, Hera of Ammon, Parammon, heroes, and the wives of heroes, and they preserve records of consultations with the oracle at Libya.

l: temple of Hera, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Hera’s temple was said to have been built by the people of Scillus in Triphylia about eight years after Oxylus became king at Elis. It is Doric, measures 63 feet in length, and contains statues and the chest of Cypselus.

l: Hera, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Hera has a temple at Olympia containing her seated statue and many other statues and offerings. Every fifth year, sixteen matrons weave a shawl for her and preside over games in her honor.

l: Hera Festival, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Hera Festival includes races for maidens of different ages, with the youngest racing first and the eldest last. Victors receive olive crowns, a portion of the heifer sacrificed to Hera, and painted representations are made for Hera.

l: sixteen matrons, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: The sixteen matrons preside over the Hera Festival, weave Hera’s shawl, and conduct two dances called Physcoa’s dance and Hippodamia’s. They were originally selected from sixteen cities to arbitrate disputes between Elis and Pisa, and in the narrator’s time two are chosen from each of the eight tribes.

l: Hippodamia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Hippodamia was said to have selected sixteen matrons and inaugurated the games for Hera in gratitude for her marriage with Pelops. The sixteen matrons also maintain a dance called Hippodamia’s.

l: Pelops, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Pelops appears in the scenes on the chest of Cypselus, where Œnomaus pursues him and Hippodamia. His horses in that scene have wings.

l: Cypselus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Cypselus was hidden by his mother in a chest at birth because the Bacchidæ were eager to find him. His descendants, the Cypselidæ, later dedicated the chest at Olympia.

l: chest of Cypselus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: The chest of Cypselus is made of cedar and decorated with figures in ivory, gold, and carved cedar. It bears old inscriptions, including writing in the ox-fashion style, and depicts mythological scenes such as the pursuit of Pelops, the games for Pelias, Hercules shooting the hydra, and the sons of Boreas driving away the Harpies.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Hercules appears among the scenes on the chest of Cypselus, seated with his wife during the games in memory of Pelias. He is also shown shooting the hydra that infested the river Amymone.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Olympian games are associated with victors who are entertained in the Town Hall of the people of Elis. The victors receive crowns made from the wild olive tree, and the Hera Festival uses a race-course at Olympia.

l: Hera’s maiden race, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: Hera’s maiden race is held at the regular race-course at Olympia but is one-sixth of a stade shorter. Maidens run with their hair down, wearing a short tunic below the knee with the right shoulder bare to the breast.

l: sacrifices at the altars, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XV.
s: The people of Elis perform sacrifices at the altars once every month. They burn frankincense and honey cakes, decorate the altars with olive branches, and pour out wine, except that wine is not offered to the Nymphs, the Mistresses, or the joint altar of all the gods.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The unit describes mythological scenes and inscriptions on the chest, including figures such as Hercules, Zeus, Atlas, Medea, and the gods and heroes of the Trojan and Theban stories; its maker is conjectured to have been Eumelus the Corinthian. It then recounts votive offerings and monuments at Olympia, Altis, and the temples, including the pillar of Oenomaus, Philip’s House, and statues made from fines imposed on dishonest athletes. Pausanias details several cases of bribery, lateness, cheating, and cowardice in the Olympic games, and explains how the resulting fines funded statues of Zeus. The account also connects the chest’s military scenes with Cypselus and his ancestors, whose origins lay beyond Sicyon.

l: chest of Cypselus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The chest bears scenes from myth, including Death and Sleep, Justice and Injustice, Helen and Menelaus, Jason and Medea, Atlas and Hercules, Achilles and Memnon, and many other figures. Its inscriptions identify or describe several scenes, and its maker is considered impossible to determine, though suspicion points to Eumelus the Corinthian.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Zeus is represented among the statues and votive offerings at Olympia, and fines imposed on dishonest athletes were used to make statues of him. The chest also contains mythological scenes connected with Zeus, including his deception of Alcmena by assuming the appearance of Amphitryon.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Hercules is identified on the chest as the armed man approaching Atlas, and he is also shown fighting Geryon and shooting Centaurs. These scenes represent feats attributed to him.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Elis imposed fines on athletes who bribed opponents, arrived too late, or otherwise violated the rules of the games. Its people also restored the temple of Hera, maintained records of Olympic victors, and erected statues from athletic fines.

l: Cypselus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Cypselus is described as a Corinthian who possessed the chest. His ancestors were said to have come from Gonussa beyond Sicyon and to descend from Melas, and the military scenes on the chest are conjectured to portray the forces of Melas.

l: Delphi, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The oracle at Delphi required the Athenians to pay the fine imposed after Callippus bribed his opponents before it would again provide them with responses. Delphi is also mentioned in connection with the oracle that Aletes initially disobeyed when he refused to admit Melas and his army.

l: Altis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Altis contains votive offerings, temples, statues of Zeus made from athletic fines, the pillar called the pillar of Oenomaus, and the Temple of the Mother. During a battle between the Lacedaemonians and Elis, the people of Elis defended themselves from the temples and other high buildings inside Altis.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Olympia is the setting for the contests, the temple buildings, and the monuments commemorating athletic victories and offenses. The quoit of Iphitus records an armistice between Elis and the Olympians, while statues at Olympia warn athletes against cheating and bribery.

l: Eupolus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Eupolus of Thessaly bribed Agenor, Prytanis, and Phormio to let him win the boxing contest. He and the athletes he bribed were fined by Elis, and six statues of Zeus were made from the money.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Olympic games are presented as contests that should be won through merit, speed, and bodily strength rather than money. Athletes were punished for bribery, accepting bribes, arriving late, and cowardice, with fines often used to erect statues of Zeus.

l: bribery at Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Bribery at Olympia involved athletes or their associates paying opponents to lose or secure a victory. The unit recounts cases involving Eupolus, Callippus, Eudelus, and the boxers Didas and Sarapammon, as well as Damonicus bribing Sosander on behalf of his son.

l: fines imposed for cheating, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Fines imposed on athletes and those responsible for their misconduct were used to create statues of Zeus and other memorials. The unit records fines for bribery, cheating, lateness, and cowardice, including the fines imposed on Eupolus and his opponents, Callippus and his opponents, and later boxers.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The unit describes numerous statues and votive offerings at Olympia, especially statues of Zeus erected by cities and individuals, together with their inscriptions, artists, and historical contexts. It records the statue dedicated by the Greeks who fought at Platæa, the 30-year peace between the Lacedæmonians and Athenians, and the oath-taking statue of Zeus in the Council Chamber. It also recounts the shipwreck of the Messenians’ chorus in the Sicilian Strait and the brazen effigies erected at Olympia in memory of the drowned boys, choir-master, and piper. Other offerings include representations of Hercules and the Achæan heroes, including works attributed to Onatas the son of Micon.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Zeus is represented by many statues and votive offerings at Olympia, made by cities and private individuals. His statues hold or are accompanied by attributes including thunderbolts, eagles, javelins, sceptres, lilies, and Ganymede, while the statue of Zeus the God of Oaths is used for formal oaths.

l: Altis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Altis contains numerous statues and votive offerings, including the largest brazen statue of Zeus, the statues of the boys from the Sicilian Strait, and several other offerings on its walls and near its temples. An altar near the entrance to the course is used by trumpeters and heralds when they proclaim the games.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Olympia contains a large collection of statues and votive offerings dedicated by Greek cities, foreign communities, and private individuals. The unit records offerings there from places including Apollonia, Metapontum, Phlius, Leontini, the Messenians at the Sicilian Strait, Agrigentum, the Achæans, and Thasos.

l: statues of Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The statues of Zeus at Olympia vary in size, appearance, attributes, and dedication. They include offerings by the people of Cynætha, Cleolas of Phlius, Apollonia, Metapontum, Phlius, Leontini, the Greeks who fought at Platæa, the Megarians, Hybla, Cleitor, Corinth, Thessaly, Psophidius, the Lacedæmonians, Mummius, Elis, the Elaitæ, and the Chersonese in Cnidus.

l: Greeks who fought at Platæa, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Greeks who fought at Platæa against Mardonius and the Medes dedicated a statue of Zeus at Olympia. The states that took part in the action were inscribed on the right side of its basement, beginning with the Lacedæmonians and followed by the Athenians and other participating communities.

l: Battle of Platæa, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Battle of Platæa is commemorated at Olympia by a statue of Zeus dedicated by the Greeks who fought against Mardonius and the Medes. The dedication lists the states that participated in the action.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Lacedæmonians are listed first among the states that fought at Platæa and dedicated a statue of Zeus after their second war with the Messenians. They also dedicated a 12-foot statue of Zeus bearing an inscription, and their citizens included the sculptors Aristo and Telestas.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Athenians are listed second among the states that fought at Platæa. They made the 30-year peace with the Lacedæmonians after their second reduction of Eubœa and retained the option of private friendship with the Argives.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Elis contains and maintains many of the statues and votive offerings described at Olympia. The people of Elis dedicated the largest brazen statue of Zeus in Altis after their war with the Arcadians, and they also brought a statue of Hercules to Olympia.

l: 30-year peace between Sparta and Athens, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The 30-year peace between the Lacedæmonians and Athenians was recorded on a brazen pillar near the statue of Zeus dedicated by the Greeks who fought at Platæa. It was made by the Athenians after their second reduction of Eubœa and excluded the Argives from sharing in the peace, while allowing private friendship between Athenians and Argives.

l: Council Chamber statue of Zeus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The statue of Zeus in the Council Chamber is called Zeus the God of Oaths and is described as the most frightening of the statues of Zeus to wicked men. It holds a thunderbolt in each hand, and athletes, their relatives and trainers, and the umpires swear before it.

l: Olympic athletes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Olympic athletes swear before Zeus the God of Oaths, over the entrails of a boar, that they will not cheat at the games. They also swear that they have trained carefully for ten months.

l: Messenians at the Sicilian Strait, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Messenians at the Sicilian Strait traditionally sent thirty-five boys, a choir-master, and a piper to Rhegium for a national feast. After all of them died in a sea disaster, they placed brazen effigies of the boys, the choir-master, and the piper at Olympia.

l: shipwreck in the Sicilian Strait, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: A vessel carrying the Messenians’ chorus, choir-master, and piper was wrecked in the Sicilian Strait, and none of those aboard survived. The account attributes the danger to the strait’s winds, meeting seas, strong swell, sea-monsters, and difficulty reaching shore.

l: Sicilian Strait, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Sicilian Strait is described as extremely stormy, where the Sicilian and Tyrrhenian seas meet and where strong ebb and flow creates a tremendous swell even in calm weather. It is also said to contain many sea-monsters and to offer shipwrecked mariners little chance of reaching safety.

l: brazen effigies of the drowned chorus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The brazen effigies of the drowned chorus, its choir-master, and its piper were erected at Olympia by the grieving Messenians at the Sicilian Strait. The effigies were made by Callon of Elis, and Hippias later composed elegiac lines for them.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Hercules appears in several votive offerings at Olympia. These include Hercules shooting at the Nemean lion, Hercules fighting an Amazon on horseback for her belt, and a ten-cubit brazen Hercules dedicated by the Thasians.

l: Achæans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Achæans dedicated statues at Olympia of the Greek heroes who drew lots to face Hector in single combat, with Nestor shown throwing the lots into his helmet. Their inscription identifies them as descendants of the divine Pelops, the son of Tantalus.

l: Onatas the Æginetan, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Onatas the son of Micon is identified as the maker of the statue of Idomeneus among the Achæan votive offerings. An inscription on Idomeneus’ shield says that Onatas made that statue and many others, and the account ranks the Æginetan Onatas among the greatest sculptors since Dædalus and the Attic school.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Dorian Messenians received Naupactus from the Athenians and erected a Victory monument at Olympia, claiming that it commemorated their participation with the Athenians in the action at Sphacteria. Olympia contained many offerings associated with Micythus, including works by Argive Glaucus and Dionysius, as well as offerings by Phormis and others. Phormis, a Mænalian who served Gelon and Hiero in Sicily, dedicated horses, charioteers, and other offerings at Olympia. The text also describes offerings and marvels in the Altis, including Phormis’s unusually alluring bronze horse and a trophy made from Lacedæmonian spoils.

l: Messenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: They received Naupactus from the Athenians and erected a Victory at Olympia on a pillar. They said the monument commemorated their participation with the Athenians in the action at Sphacteria, though they omitted the enemy’s name because they feared the Lacedæmonians.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: They gave Naupactus to the Dorian Messenians. The Messenians claimed that they had shared with the Athenians in the action at Sphacteria.

l: Victory, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: It was a Victory erected on a pillar at Olympia, designed by the Mendæan Pæonius and made from spoils taken from an enemy, according to the narrator’s impression. The Messenians said it commemorated their share with the Athenians in the action at Sphacteria and did not name the enemy.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: It contained numerous votive offerings, including offerings of Micythus, the Victory of the Dorian Messenians, Phormis’s horses and charioteers, and other dedications by communities and individuals. Its Altis also contained a trophy made from Lacedæmonian spoils and other bronze monuments.

l: Micythus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: He placed many votive offerings at Olympia, including works by Argive Glaucus and Dionysius. The inscriptions identify him as the son of Chœrus and a native of Rhegium, and state that his offerings fulfilled a vow for the recovery of his son from a wasting consumption. Herodotus is said to have reported that Micythus was the slave and treasurer of Anaxilas, later went to Tegea, and that Nero removed some of his offerings.

l: Argive Glaucus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: He made several works among Micythus’s offerings at Olympia, including Amphitrite, Poseidon, Vesta, Proserpine, Aphrodite, Ganymede, Artemis, Homer, Hesiod, Æsculapius, and Hygiea. He also made the statue of Athene that stood near the larger offerings of Micythus.

l: Phormis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: He was a Mænalian from Mænalus who went to Sicily to serve Gelon and later Hiero, displaying great valor and becoming wealthy. He dedicated offerings at Olympia and Delphi, including two horses with charioteers, and an image of himself fighting several enemies; the latter was actually dedicated by the Syracusan Lycortas out of affection for him.

l: horses and charioteers of Phormis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Phormis’s offerings at Olympia consisted of two horses and two charioteers, with one charioteer beside each horse. The first horse and groom were made by Dionysius the Argive, and the second by the Æginetan Simo.

l: Phormis’s horse, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: One of Phormis’s bronze horses bore an inscription identifying it as dedicated by Phormis the Arcadian from Mænalus, then a Syracusan. Though inferior in size and beauty to many horses at Olympia and damaged by the loss of its tail, it irresistibly aroused stallions, which repeatedly tried to mount it until restrained by force or whips; the narrator attributes this to a magician’s cunning.

l: Phormis’s votive offerings, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: They stood among the votive offerings at Olympia and included two horses, two charioteers, and an image of Phormis fighting one, two, and even three enemies. The Greeks called Lycortas’s fighting image part of Phormis’s offerings, although its inscription identified Lycortas as the dedicator.

l: Altis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: It contained Phormis’s bronze horse, which stallions repeatedly entered or rushed toward in attempts to mount it. Under its plane trees stood a bronze trophy dedicated by the people of Elis from Lacedæmonian spoils, and it also contained the offerings of the Mendæans and other monuments.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Pausanias describes statues and other votive offerings at Olympia, especially those commemorating athletes, horsemen, trainers, rulers, and military figures. He records the victories, origins, artists, inscriptions, and unusual histories of many Olympic contestants, including Lichas, Damiscus, Dicon, Sostratus, and Lysander. He also discusses Elis's control of the games, disputes over athletic records, the Messenians' return to success after their restoration, and the shifting loyalties of the Samians and other Ionians after the Battle of Aegospotami.

l: Pausanias, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Pausanias explains that his subject is not a complete catalogue of Olympic victors but an account of statues and other votive offerings. He records inscriptions, traditions, artists, athletic victories, and uncertainties concerning figures such as Oebotas and Aristotle.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Olympia contains numerous statues, chariots, votive offerings, and inscriptions commemorating athletes, horse-breeders, rulers, seers, and military figures. Its games and records are repeatedly used to establish the victories and origins of the people represented.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Elis supplied many athletes and horsemen whose statues stood at Olympia, and its people controlled the recording and administration of the games. The Eleans excluded their own people from the Isthmian games and did not record the 104th Olympiad because it was conducted by the Pisæans and Arcadians.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: The Olympic contests included running, wrestling, boxing, the pancratium, the pentathlum, horse-races, and chariot-races. The unit records disputes, exclusions, changing rules, and the victories of contestants from many Greek communities.

l: votive offerings, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Pausanias's account focuses on votive offerings, especially statues and related monuments dedicated at Olympia. These offerings commemorate athletic victories, rulers, military achievements, and honored individuals.

l: Lysippus, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Lysippus made the statue of Troilus, the Elean victor in the chariot-race, and the statue of a pancratiast from Acarnania named Xenarches. His work is also used by Pausanias to date the possible war in which Chilon of Patræ died.

l: Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: After the invasion of the Medes, the Lacedæmonians devoted themselves more than other Greeks to breeding horses. They erected statues of Spartan horse-breeders and sent a statue of Archidamus to Olympia; they also invaded Elis under Agis because of the treatment of Lichas.

l: Lichas, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Lichas entered the chariot-race as a Theban while the Lacedæmonians were excluded, then bound the victorious charioteer with a riband. The umpires scourged him, and the Lacedæmonians under Agis invaded Elis because of this incident; Lichas later erected his statue at Olympia.

l: Altis, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Altis contained the statues and monuments described by Pausanias, including those of athletes, horsemen, and seers. A fight took place there during the Lacedæmonian invasion of Elis, and Dædalus later erected a trophy for the Eleans after their victory over the Laconians.

l: Messenians, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: When the Messenians were exiles from the Peloponnese, their success at Olympia also failed, apart from Leontiscus and Symmachus, whom the Sicilians disputed as Messenians. After their return to the Peloponnese, their Olympic success returned, beginning with Damiscus's victory in the boys' course.

l: Lysander, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: The Samians erected a statue at Olympia to Lysander, son of Aristocritus, and dedicated inscriptions praising his fame. After the Athenian fleet was defeated at Aegospotami, the Ephesians also placed statues of Lysander and other Spartans in the temple of Artemis.

l: Alcibiades, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: When Alcibiades had a strong Athenian fleet near Ionia, most of the Ionians courted him, and the Samians displayed a brazen bust of him in the temple of Hera. Their support changed after the Athenian defeat at Aegospotami.

l: statues of Olympic victors, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: Not every Olympic victor had a statue, and Pausanias says that some received statues because of greater renown or superior artistic quality rather than simply because they won. The statues record athletic achievements, origins, patrons, artists, inscriptions, and sometimes unusual events surrounding the victories.

l: pentathlum, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: The pentathlum appears among the contests recorded at Olympia, Delphi, and Nemea. Athletes such as Stomius, Hysmon, Eupolemus, Antiochus, and Dicon are described as winning pentathlum victories, while Hysmon trained for it to strengthen his constitution after suffering a discharge.

l: battle of Ægos-potamoi, Description of Greece, BOOK VI.--ELIS. PART II.
s: After the Athenian fleet was defeated at Aegospotami, the Samians dedicated a statue of Lysander at Olympia and the Ephesians honored Lysander and other Spartans. When Conon later won at Cnidus and Mount Dorium, the Ionians shifted their allegiance again and honored Conon and Timotheus.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: The unit describes the statue of Polydamas by Lysippus and recounts the extraordinary strength and exploits of Polydamas, son of Nicias, who was from Scotusa. Polydamas slew a lion, seized a bull, stopped a chariot, and killed three Persian Immortals in single combat at the court of Darius. Scotusa was destroyed by Alexander the king of the Pheræans, and its surviving people later suffered further losses and abandoned the town. Polydamas eventually died when he tried to hold up the collapsing roof of a cave.

l: statue of Polydamas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: The statue stands on a lofty pedestal at Olympia and was made by Lysippus. Its base and inscription record some of Polydamas's exploits.

l: Polydamas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Polydamas, the son of Nicias and a native of Scotusa, is described as the largest man of his time. He won notable victories in the pancratium, slew a lion unarmed, seized a powerful bull, stopped a speeding chariot, and killed three Persian Immortals in single combat at Susa. He died after remaining beneath the cracking roof of a cave and attempting to hold up the falling rock.

l: Scotusa, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Scotusa was the native place of Polydamas. Alexander the king of the Pheræans destroyed it while its people were gathered in the theatre, and the town was later left deserted by the few survivors.

l: people of Scotusa, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: The people of Scotusa were surrounded in their theatre by Alexander the king of the Pheræans, who killed the gathered men and sold the women and children. The few who escaped were reduced further and eventually left the town.

l: Alexander the king of the Pheræans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Alexander the king of the Pheræans attacked Scotusa during a time of peace while its people were gathered in the theatre. He killed the men who were there and sold the women and children, using the proceeds to maintain a mercenary army.

l: pancratium, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: The pancratium had several competitors with notable victories, including Polydamas, who gained crowns in the event.

l: lions, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Lions lived in the mountainous part of Thrace inside the river Nestus and sometimes prowled near Mount Olympus. They once attacked the army of Xerxes and killed many of the camels carrying grain, and Polydamas later slew a large lion on Mount Olympus.

l: Mount Olympus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Mount Olympus was frequented by lions and had one side facing Macedonia and another facing Thessaly and the river Peneus. Polydamas killed a large lion there while unarmed.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Hercules is said to have defeated the Nemean lion. Polydamas slew a lion on Mount Olympus in an attempt to emulate Hercules.

l: Darius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Darius, the illegitimate son of Artaxerxes, deposed Sogdius with the help of the Persian commonalty and became king. After hearing of Polydamas's exploits, he summoned him to his court at Susa by promising rewards.

l: Persians called Immortals, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Three Persians called Immortals challenged Polydamas at Susa, and he slew all three in single combat.

l: cave, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Polydamas entered a cave in summer with several companions. When its roof cracked and threatened to collapse, his companions fled, but Polydamas stayed and was crushed beneath the falling rock.

l: death of Polydamas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER V.
s: Polydamas's death fulfilled the warning that excessive confidence in strength could bring ruin. He was crushed to death after trying to hold up the collapsing roof of a cave while his companions escaped.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit describes statues and athletic victories at Olympia, especially those of Euthymus, Diagoras and his family, and other Greek athletes. Euthymus defeated the boxer Theagenes in one Olympiad, later won three Olympic boxing crowns, and defeated the Hero of Temesa, after which he married the maiden offered to the Hero. Diagoras of Rhodes and his descendants achieved exceptional success in boxing and the pancratium, while Dorieus also became involved in conflicts between Rhodes, Sparta, Athens, and the great king. The text also recounts legends connected with Temesa, Pisirodus, and Glaucus of Carystus.

l: Diagoras, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Diagoras of Rhodes won the Olympic boxing victory among men, and his statue was made by the Megarian Callicles. He came to Olympia with his sons Acusilaus and Damagetus and was carried on their shoulders after their victories; he was descended on his mother's side from Aristomenes.

l: Euthymus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Euthymus was a boxer from Locri near the promontory of Zephyrium, reputed by local people to be the son of the River Cæcinus rather than Astycles. He won Olympic boxing victories in the 74th, 76th, and 77th Olympiads, defeated the Hero of Temesa, married the maiden offered to the Hero, and was said to have lived to an advanced age without dying like other men.

l: Theagenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Theagenes of Thasos outboxed Euthymus while attempting to win both the boxing and pancratium prizes in the same Olympiad. Because he was exhausted in the boxing contest, he did not receive the pancratium crown and was fined two talents, one for offending the god and one for injuring Euthymus; he paid the divine fine in the 76th Olympiad and thereafter did not compete again as a boxer.

l: Temesa, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Temesa was the Italian town where the ghost of a sailor killed for violating a maiden had long slain its inhabitants. After Euthymus defeated the Hero associated with the ghost, Temesa was freed from the trouble, and the text says that it was still inhabited.

l: Acusilaus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Acusilaus, a son of Diagoras, won the Olympic boxing prize among men. He and his brother Damagetus came to Olympia with their father and carried him in celebration after their victories.

l: Dorieus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Dorieus, the youngest son of Diagoras, won three successive Olympic pancratium victories, as well as victories at the Isthmian, Nemean, and Pythian games. He was entered as a Thurian for some contests after migrating from Rhodes to Thurii, later returned to Rhodes, fought for Spartan interests against Athens, was captured and released by the Athenians, and was eventually condemned and executed by the Spartans according to Androtion.

l: Damagetus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Damagetus, a son of Diagoras, won the pancratium at Olympia before his brother Dorieus surpassed him with three victories. He came to Olympia with Diagoras and Acusilaus and helped carry their father in celebration.

l: Pisirodus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Pisirodus, the son of Callipatira and grandson of Diagoras, won the Olympic boxing prize among boys. His mother disguised herself as a trainer and dressed him as a man to bring him to the games, and he had a statue near his maternal grandfather's statue at Olympia.

l: Glaucus of Carystus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Glaucus of Carystus was said to have come originally from Anthedon in Bœotia and to be descended from Glaucus the sea-god. Originally a husbandman, he used his hand to replace a ploughshare and later became a boxer; he won twice at the Pythian games and eight times at the Nemean and Isthmian games. His statue, made by Glaucias the Æginetan and erected by his son, shows him boxing, and the people of Carystus said he was buried on an island called Glaucus' island.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Olympia contains the statues and votive monuments described in this unit, including those of Euthymus, Diagoras and his family, and many other athletes. It is also the place where the athletes' Olympic victories were proclaimed and commemorated.

l: Rhodes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Rhodes was the home of Diagoras and his family, including Dorieus. Dorieus and Pisirodus were entered as Thurians after faction drove them from Rhodes, although Dorieus later returned; Rhodes was also persuaded by Conon to revolt from the Lacedæmonians and join the Athenians and the great king.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Olympic Games awarded crowns and prizes in boxing, wrestling, pancratium, running, the pentathlum, and chariot racing. The unit records the victories of Euthymus, Diagoras and his descendants, Glaucus of Carystus, and many other athletes, as well as the erection of statues and chariots commemorating them.

l: Diagorid family, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Diagorid family included Diagoras, his sons Acusilaus, Damagetus, and Dorieus, and his descendants Eucles and Pisirodus. Its members achieved numerous victories at Olympia and other games, and statues of the family were displayed together at Olympia.

l: statue of Euthymus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The statue of Euthymus was made by Pythagoras and is described as especially fine. It stood near the statues of other athletes at Olympia.

l: statues of Diagoras and his family, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The statues of Diagoras and his family stood together at Olympia in an ordered group: Acusilaus, Dorieus, Damagetus, and Diagoras. The statue of Diagoras was made by Callicles, while the text also mentions the statue of Pisirodus near his maternal grandfather.

l: Hero of Temesa, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Hero of Temesa was the ghost of a sailor stoned to death after violating a maiden. The people of Temesa annually offered him the handsomest girl in the town until Euthymus fought and defeated him; the Hero then dived into the sea and was never seen again. A painting showed him as a dark, formidable figure in a wolfskin and named him Lycas.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The unit describes Theagenes of Thasos, his legendary strength, athletic victories, and later honors. After his death, a statue of Theagenes killed one of his enemies, was thrown into the sea, and was eventually recovered and restored when a famine afflicted Thasos. Delphi instructed the Thasians to restore those they had exiled, and the Pythian Priestess later told them they had forgotten Theagenes. The Thasians then sacrificed to the statue as to a god, and Theagenes received honors as a healer.

l: Theagenes of Thasos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Theagenes was said by the Thasians to be the son of Hercules disguised as Timosthenes. As a boy, he became famous for carrying away a bronze statue, and he later won numerous athletic victories, including three at the Pythian games, nine at Nemea, ten at the Isthmus, and many others, for a total of 1,400 crowns. After his death, he was honored in various parts of Greece and among the barbarians, and was believed to cure diseases.

l: Thasos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: Thasos was the home of Theagenes and of the citizens who first punished his statue by throwing it into the sea. When the land yielded no fruit, the Thasians consulted Delphi, recalled some exiles, recovered the statue, and restored it to its original site, after which they sacrificed to it as to a god.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: At Olympia, Theagenes had notable athletic exploits, including defeating Euthymus in boxing and later defeating Dromeus of Mantinea in the pancratium. The text states that his most notable exploits at Olympia had already been recorded.

l: statue of Theagenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: After Theagenes died, one of his enemies scourged his statue nightly, and the statue eventually fell on and killed him. The Thasians prosecuted the statue for murder and threw it into the sea, but fishermen later recovered it; the Thasians restored it and sacrificed to it as to a god. The statue in the Altis was made by the Aeginetan Glaucias.

l: Thasian famine, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: When the earth yielded no fruit to the Thasians, they treated the resulting dearth as a divine problem and consulted Delphi. The famine continued after they recalled some exiles, and the oracle attributed the unresolved situation to their having forgotten Theagenes.

l: Delphi, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Thasians sent envoys to Delphi during the famine. Delphi first instructed them to restore those who had been banished and later gave the message that they had forgotten Theagenes.

l: Pythian Priestess, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Pythian Priestess told the Thasians, "Your great Theagenes you have forgotten," after their first response to the oracle had not ended the dearth.

l: worship of Theagenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XI.
s: After the statue of Theagenes was recovered and restored, the Thasians sacrificed to it as to a god. Theagenes also received various honors from the people of Thasos and was regarded as able to cure diseases.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: The unit describes monuments at Olympia commemorating victories associated with Hiero the son of Dinomenes, Hiero the son of Hierocles, and other figures. Hiero the son of Hierocles became tyrant of Syracuse, shifted allegiance from Carthage to Rome during the war for Sicily, and was assassinated by Dinomenes. The passage also records statues and victories of Areus, the son of Acrotatus, Aratus the son of Clinias, and several athletes. It discusses inscriptions identifying victors and corrects the claim that Tritaea was an Arcadian town.

l: Hiero, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: He was tyrant of Syracuse after his brother Gelon and won victories in the Olympian contests. Memorials of his victories included a brazen chariot, race-horses, and boys on the horses, although these offerings were made by Dinomenes the son of Hiero rather than by Hiero himself.

l: Hiero the son of Hierocles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: He was also tyrant of Syracuse and rose to power after the death of Agathocles in the second year of the 126th Olympiad. He first supported the Carthaginians in the war for Sicily but soon joined the Romans, believing their power stronger and more lasting. He was assassinated by Dinomenes, and his sons dedicated statues of him at Olympia.

l: Areus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: He was king of the Lacedæmonians. Olympia contained a statue of him and a second statue of him on horseback; one was dedicated by the men of Elis.

l: Aratus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: A statue of him at Olympia was a votive offering of the Corinthians. He was also proclaimed victor at Olympia in the chariot-race.

l: Syracuse, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Syracuse was ruled by Hiero the son of Dinomenes and later by Hiero the son of Hierocles. After Hiero the son of Hierocles was assassinated, Dinomenes tried to kill Hippocrates, who had come to Syracuse from Erbessus and was attempting to persuade the people.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Olympia contained monuments and statues honoring Hiero the son of Dinomenes, Hiero the son of Hierocles, Areus, Aratus, and other victors. The monuments included chariots, horses, and statues made or dedicated by various individuals and communities.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Elis was associated with the dedication of a statue of Areus by its men. Timon, the son of Ægyptus, was also a native of Elis and had a brazen chariot at Olympia.

l: Olympian contests, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: Hiero the son of Dinomenes was commemorated for victories in the Olympian contests. Aratus was proclaimed victor at Olympia in the chariot-race, and the inscription for Agesarchus states that he defeated men in boxing at the Olympian games.

l: war between Rome and Carthage for Sicily, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: During the war, the Carthaginians controlled more than half of Sicily. Hiero the son of Hierocles initially joined the Carthaginians but changed sides and joined the Romans after judging Roman power to be stronger and more lasting.

l: chariot of Hiero, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: The brazen chariot commemorating Hiero the son of Dinomenes stood at Olympia with race-horses and boys on the horses at each side. Onatas the Æginetan made the chariot, while Calamis made the horses and the boys; Dinomenes the son of Hiero offered the monument to the god.

l: statues of Hiero the son of Hierocles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XII.
s: His sons erected two statues of him at Olympia, one on horseback and the other on foot. Both were made by Mico the Syracusan, the son of Niceratus.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The unit describes numerous victors and monuments at Olympia, including Astylus of Croton, Hermogenes Xanthius, Polites, Leonidas of Rhodes, Milo, Clitomachus of Thebes, and Caprus of Elis. It records athletic achievements in running, wrestling, boxing, the pancratium, the pentathlum, horse-racing, and chariot-racing, together with the sculptors and dedicators of many statues. It also discusses unusual athletic feats, disputed victory records, the careers and deaths of athletes, and the political or military associations of several figures. The account repeatedly compares Olympic victories with successes at the Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Olympic games are presented through records of victories in running, wrestling, boxing, the pancratium, the pentathlum, horse-racing, and chariot-racing. The unit also records disputes about Olympic victory lists, including the victories attributed to the sons of Phidolas.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Elis controlled admission to contests and proclaimed victors at Olympia. Its people rejected Pherias as too young in the 78th Olympiad, later allowed him to wrestle among the boys, and proclaimed Phidolas victorious after his mare Aura completed the race without its rider.

l: Artemidorus of Tralles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Artemidorus of Tralles was too young to win the pancratium among the boys at Olympia, but later defeated the boys, the unbearded competitors, and the best men at Smyrna on the same day. He won the Olympic pancratium among men in the 212th Olympiad.

l: Milo, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Milo of Croton won six Olympic wrestling prizes, one among boys, and came to Olympia seeking a seventh victory but was defeated by Timasitheus. He was said to have carried his statue to the Altis and to have performed feats involving a pomegranate, an oiled quoit, a cord around his forehead, and the immobilization of a finger; he was later killed by wolves after becoming trapped in a split tree.

l: Clitomachus of Thebes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Clitomachus won wrestling, boxing, and pancratium prizes at the Isthmian games and three pancratium victories at the Pythian games. At Olympia he was second to Theagenes of Thasos in boxing and the pancratium before winning the pancratium in the 141st Olympiad; he later lost that contest to Caprus after asking that it be held before boxing battered him.

l: Caprus of Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Caprus of Elis won wrestling and pancratium prizes on the same day, the first recorded athlete to do so. He defeated Clitomachus in the pancratium and Pæanius in wrestling, and two statues of him stood at Olympia.

l: Nemean games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Nemean games are mentioned in comparisons of athletes' records. Nicasylus of Rhodes was proclaimed victor there, Tisander had victories there according to the account's context, and the Argives were said not to have kept records of Nemean victors at an earlier time.

l: Pythian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Pythian games are repeatedly compared with the Olympic games. Tisander had four boxing victories there, Milo had six victories among men and one among boys, Clitomachus won three pancratium victories, and several other athletes are recorded as winning in wrestling, boxing, the pentathlum, or running.

l: Isthmian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Isthmian games are listed with the Olympic, Pythian, and Nemean games in accounts of an athlete's complete record. Nicasylus was proclaimed victor there, Epitherses won two boxing victories, and Lycus won once with the horse of Phidolas.

l: pentathlum, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The pentathlum is recorded as an event in which Gorgus of Elis won four Olympic victories, as well as one victory in the double course and one in the race in heavy armour. Timon won the pentathlum at all the Greek games except the Isthmian, and several other athletes in the unit are recorded as pentathlum victors.

l: pancratium, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The pancratium appears as both a boys' and men's event. Artemidorus, Clitomachus, and Caprus are especially noted for victories or contests in it, while Aristophon of Athens, Theagenes of Thasos, and other athletes are also associated with pancratium victories.

l: statues of Olympic victors, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The unit describes many statues at Olympia, identifying their subjects, dedicators, and sculptors when known. The statues commemorate athletes, rulers, soldiers, horses, and political figures, and some inscriptions preserve athletic records or other information about the people represented.

l: Altis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Altis contains the statues and pillars described throughout the unit. Milo was said to have carried his own statue there, Pyrrhus had a statue erected there by Thrasybulus of Elis, and Dinosthenes set up a pillar there recording a distance to another pillar at Lacedæmon.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The unit describes monuments, statues, votive offerings, and treasuries in and around Altis at Olympia, including those honoring athletes, rulers, and notable figures such as Gorgias of Leontini and Anaximenes of Lampsacus. It recounts the treasuries of several Greek cities and the objects preserved in them, including the treasury of the Sicyonians. It also describes Mount Cronos, the temple of Ilithyia and Sosipolis, the Hippodamium, and the arrangements for the Olympian games. Finally, it explains the horse-race starting-place, the horse races, and the various traditions concerning Taraxippus, the terror of horses.

l: Altis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Altis contains numerous statues, votive offerings, city treasuries, temples, the Hippodamium, and facilities associated with the Olympian games. The unit describes its processional entrance, the surrounding monuments, and objects dedicated by communities and individuals.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Olympia is presented as the site of the Altis, the treasuries, athletic statues, the Olympian games, and the horse-racing facilities. It contains dedications from cities and peoples including the Sicyonians, Carthaginians, Epidamnus, Sybaris, Cyrene, Metapontum, Megara, and Gela.

l: Gorgias of Leontini, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Gorgias of Leontini had a statue at Olympia placed there by Eumolpus, his relative through marriage. He was the son of Carmantides and was said to have been the first to practise rhetoric, to have been famous for eloquence at the festival at Olympia, to have gone with Tisias on an embassy to the Athenians, and to have lived 105 years.

l: Anaximenes of Lampsacus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Anaximenes had a statue at Olympia through the honor of the people of Lampsacus. He persuaded Alexander to pardon Lampsacus by asking him, under oath, to enslave its people and destroy the city; he also wrote histories, practised extempore oratory, and composed a work imitating Theopompus that brought hatred upon Theopompus.

l: Mount Cronos, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Mount Cronos lies behind the base holding the treasuries and extends along their length. Those called the Basilæ sacrifice to Cronos on its summit at the vernal equinox in the month of Elaphius.

l: treasuries of Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The treasuries of Olympia stand on a tufa-stone base north of the temple of Hera, with Mount Cronos behind them. The unit describes treasuries belonging to the Sicyonians, Carthaginians, Epidamnus, Sybaris, Cyrene, Metapontum, Megara, and Gela, together with their dedications and inscriptions.

l: treasury of the Sicyonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The treasury of the Sicyonians was the offering of Myron, king of the Sicyonians, after his chariot victory in the 33rd Olympiad. It had Doric and Ionic chambers of brass and contained athletic equipment, armour dedicated by the Myanes, the sword of Pelops, the horn of Amalthea, and a boxwood statue of Apollo.

l: Ilithyia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Ilithyia was honored in a temple at the northern end of Mount Cronos and was surnamed the Olympian. She was worshipped jointly with Sosipolis because the Eleans believed that she had introduced the child who became Sosipolis into the world.

l: Sosipolis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Sosipolis was the tutelary deity of the people of Elis and was honored inside the temple of Ilithyia. According to the story, he appeared as a dragon from a baby offered to aid the Eleans, causing the Arcadians to flee and enabling the Eleans to win a notable victory.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Elis had many victorious athletes represented by statues at Olympia and maintained the worship of Sosipolis and Ilithyia. Its people defeated an invading Arcadian army after the transformation of the offered child into a dragon, and they removed the Hesperides from the treasury of Epidamnus to the temple of Hera.

l: Hippodamium, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Hippodamium was an enclosure inside Altis, surrounded by a wall and occupying about an acre. Women entered it each year to sacrifice to Hippodamia and perform other rites in her honor.

l: Hippodamia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Hippodamia was honored in the Hippodamium, where women performed annual rites for her. She was said to have fled to Midea after Pelops became angry with her over the death of Chrysippus, and her remains were later placed at Olympia; a statue of her also stood near one of the goals of the course.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Olympian games were watched by the priestess of Demeter Chamyne from an altar of white stone opposite the umpires. The games included athletic contests and horse races, and the horse-racing starts were organized so that all competitors could begin fairly.

l: horse-race starting-place, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The horse-race starting-place was shaped like the prow of a ship, with its beak turned toward the course, and each side was more than 400 feet long. It had buildings assigned by lot to entrants, ropes that were released in sequence, a brazen dolphin, and an altar bearing a mechanical brazen eagle that rose when the start was signaled.

l: horse-races, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The horse races began by releasing the ropes for the horses positioned along the starting-place in sequence until all could start together at the beak. Charioteers and horses then demonstrated their skill and speed, but they were endangered by the fear caused by Taraxippus.

l: Taraxippus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Taraxippus was a circular altar or place at the outlet of the horse-racing course that suddenly terrified horses, often causing chariots to break apart and charioteers to be injured. The Greeks offered several explanations for it, including that it was connected with Olenius, Dameon, Myrtilus, Oenomaus, Alcathous, or Poseidon Hippius; the narrator considered the last explanation most plausible.

l: battle between the Eleans and Arcadians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: During the battle between the Eleans and Arcadians, a woman offered her baby to help Elis according to a dream. The child became a dragon, frightening the Arcadians and allowing the Eleans to pursue them and win a notable victory; a monument to the Arcadians slain in the battle stood on a hill west of the Cladeus.

l: Arcadians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Arcadians invaded Elis with an army but fled after the child offered by a woman was transformed into a dragon. Those who were killed had a monument on the hill toward the west after crossing the Cladeus.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The unit describes landmarks, temples, rivers, tombs, and athletic facilities around Olympia, Pisa, and Elis. It recounts the destruction of Pisa by Elis after repeated disputes over control of the Olympian games, and it identifies monuments associated with Pelops, Hippodamia, Oinomaus, and her suitors. It also details the gymnasium, market-place, temples, porticoes, and religious practices of Elis. Several local traditions explain the names and histories of rivers, sanctuaries, statues, and towns.

l: Olympia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: At Olympia, athletes practise for the pentathlum and races in the gymnasium, and a smaller enclosure is used for wrestling. The route from Olympia passes the tomb of Oinomaus, the ruins of Pylos, Heraclea, and other sites before reaching Elis.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Elis controlled Olympia and repeatedly opposed Pisa's attempts to conduct the Olympian games. Its notable sites include an old gymnasium, several athletic enclosures, a market-place, temples, porticoes, the Umpires' Hall, and sanctuaries of Aphrodite, Pluto, Fortune, and other gods.

l: Hercules, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Hercules is associated with several places in the unit: he killed the robber Saurus, had a temple near Saurus's tomb, and is said to have exercised in the Colonnade at Elis. He also destroyed Pylos in Elis, cooperated with Athene in an attack on Pylos, and was opposed there by Pluto.

l: Pisa, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Pisa formerly controlled the boundaries and district near Olympia but later lost them to Elis. Its people repeatedly challenged Elis over the Olympian games, allied with neighboring communities, and were eventually defeated when Elis razed Pisa and the towns that supported it.

l: Pelops, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Pelops is associated with Pisa, where a building containing his remains stood near the temple of Artemis Cordace. He is said to have offered annual funeral rites to the suitors of Hippodamia and to have built their common tomb after defeating Oinomaus.

l: suitors of Hippodamia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The suitors of Hippodamia were killed by Oinomaus before Pelops defeated him. Pelops gave them a common sepulchre, and the text names many of them, including Alcathous, Euryalus, Eurymachus, Crotalus, Acrias, Capetus, Lycurgus, Lasius, Chalcodon, Tricolonus, Aristomachus, Prias, Pelagon, Aëolius, and Cronius.

l: Hippodamia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Hippodamia was the woman whose suitors were killed by Oinomaus before Pelops won the race against him. Pelops' burial of the suitors together was presented partly as an act of affection for Hippodamia.

l: Olympian games, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Pisa challenged Elis's control of the Olympian games by inviting Phido of Argos to oversee them in the eighth Olympiad and by holding games under Pantaleon in the thirty-fourth Olympiad. Games conducted by Pisa, and later by the Arcadians in the 104th Olympiad, were not included by Elis in its registers.

l: Alpheus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Alpheus flows through the district of Pylos in Elis, which the people of Elis identify with the Pylos mentioned in Homer. It also receives the rivers Diagon and Lucyanias, and a local story says that Alpheus pursued Artemis at Letrini but failed to distinguish her from the mud-covered Nymphs.

l: gymnasium of Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The gymnasium of Elis is an old training complex where athletes prepare before going to Olympia. It contains the Colonnade, racecourses, the Plethrium for testing athletes, altars and statues, the Square for wrestling, Maltho for the lads, and the Lalichmium council chamber for rhetorical practice and public criticism of writings.

l: market-place of Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The market-place of Elis, also called the Hippodrome, is built in an antique style with porticoes and regular streets, and people exercise horses there. It includes the Umpires' Hall, the Doric South Portico, the Corcyræan Portico, altars, temples and statues of Apollo, the Sun, the Moon, the Graces, Eros, Silenus, Fortune, and Pluto, as well as a room where sixteen matrons weave Hera's shawl.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The unit describes Elis, where the old theatre between the marketplace and the temple of Mene is identified with the theatre and temple of Dionysus. The people of Elis honor Dionysus above all other gods and celebrate the Thyia, during which sealed empty flagons are said to become full of wine. It also discusses Cyllene, its temples, and its harbor, as well as the Seres, the Ser insect, and the production of their thread. Finally, it gives the boundary between Elis and Achaia as the river Larisus in the present day and the promontory Araxus in ancient times.

l: temple of Dionysus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The temple of Dionysus is identified with the old theatre between the marketplace and the temple of the goddess Mene at Elis. Its statue of Dionysus is said to be by Praxiteles.

l: Dionysus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The people of Elis honor Dionysus more than any other god and say that he frequents the Thyia festival held in his honor.

l: Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Elis has a theatre and temple of Dionysus, a temple of Athene in its citadel, and the harbor of Cyllene about 120 stades away. Its country is fertile, especially for flax, and its present boundary with Achaia is the river Larisus.

l: people of Elis, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The people of Elis honor Dionysus above all other gods. They celebrate the Thyia and report that wine appears miraculously in sealed flagons during the festival.

l: Thyia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Thyia is a festival of Dionysus celebrated by the people of Elis about 8 stades from the city. During it, three empty flagons are sealed in a chapel, and the next day they are found full of wine.

l: wine, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: At the Thyia, three empty flagons are said to become full of wine while sealed inside a chapel. The people of Andros likewise say that wine flows spontaneously from the temple during their annual festival of Dionysus.

l: Cyllene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Cyllene lies about 120 stades from Elis, faces Sicily, and has a fine harbor for ships. Its dockyard belongs to the people of Elis, and the town has temples of Æsculapius and Aphrodite and an ithyphallic statue of Hermes.

l: Seres, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Seres produce the thread used for their garments from the Ser insect rather than from a plant. They breed the insects, feed them for four years on grain and in the fifth year on green reed, and then obtain the thread from the insects after they die.

l: Ser, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Greeks call the insect that produces the Seres' thread the Ser, while the Seres use another name. It is described as about twice the size of the largest beetle, resembling a web-weaving spider, and having eight feet.

l: Seria, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Seria is said to be an island in the Red Sea, although another tradition says that it is formed by a river called the Ser rather than by the sea. The Seres are said to be of Ethiopian race, while another account makes them a mixture of Scythians and Indians.

l: Achaia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Achaia borders Elis at the river Larisus in the writer's time. In ancient times, the boundary was said to have been the promontory Araxus near the sea.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The country between Elis and Sicyonia was called Achaia in Pausanias's day, but was formerly known as Ægialus and inhabited by Ægialians or Ionian Ægialians. Xuthus's sons Achæus and Ion became connected with Thessaly and Ægialus, while Ion ruled the Ægialians, founded Helice, and gave them the additional name Ionians. After the Dorians expelled the Achæans from Argos and Lacedæmon, the Achæans under Tisamenus fought the Ionians, defeated them, and settled in Ægialus. The Ionians later migrated to Attica, where the Athenians and their king Melanthus welcomed them.

l: Achaia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Achaia is the name used in Pausanias's day for the country between Elis and Sicyonia bordering the Corinthian Gulf. Its inhabitants gave the country this name.

l: Sicyonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Sicyonia borders Achaia on the east. Its inhabitants attributed the ancient name Ægialus to Ægialeus, king of what was then Sicyonia.

l: Ægialus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Ægialus was the ancient name of the country later called Achaia. The name was said either to derive from Ægialeus or from the country's mostly seashore position, and it remained in use for a long time.

l: Ægialians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Ægialians were the ancient inhabitants of Ægialus. They were also called Ionian Ægialians after Ion, and later the Achæans expelled them from the region.

l: Xuthus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Xuthus was driven out of Thessaly by his brothers, who accused him of secretly taking their father's money. He fled to Athens, married a daughter of Erechtheus, and had two sons, Achæus and Ion; he later lived and died in Ægialus.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Athens received Xuthus after he fled Thessaly, and Xuthus married a daughter of Erechtheus there. Athens later joined Ægialus in providing Achæus with an army, invited Ion to command its forces during the war with the Eleusinians, and welcomed the Ionians as settlers.

l: Achæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Achæus was the son of Xuthus and a descendant of Hellen. He took an army from Ægialus and Athens, returned to Thessaly, and recovered his ancestral throne; his sons Archander and Architeles later became connected with Argos and Lacedæmon.

l: Ion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Ion was the son of Xuthus and became the adopted son and heir of Selinus after marrying Selinus's daughter Helice. He ruled the Ægialians, founded Helice, gave the Ægialians the additional name Ionians, and later died in Attica while serving as commander for Athens.

l: Selinus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Selinus was king of the Ægialians. He offered his only child Helice in marriage to Ion and adopted Ion as his son and heir.

l: Helice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Helice was the only child of Selinus and became Ion's wife. Ion founded the city of Helice and named it after her; it later served as the place where the defeated Ionians took refuge.

l: Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Ionians were the former Ægialians, whose name was added after Ion ruled them. They opposed the Achæans' proposal to become their colonists, fought them, were besieged in Helice, and later migrated to Attica.

l: Attica, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Attica was where Ion died and was buried at Potamos. It later received the Ionians as settlers when they migrated from Ægialus.

l: Dorians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Dorians drove the Achæans and their king Tisamenus out of Argos and Lacedæmon. Their presence led the displaced Achæans to seek settlement among the Ionians.

l: Lacedæmon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Lacedæmon was one of the two Peloponnesian regions whose inhabitants were called Achæans before the Dorians returned. The Dorians expelled the Achæans from Lacedæmon, and the Lacedæmonians later removed Tisamenus's remains to Sparta in accordance with a Delphic oracle.

l: Argos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Argos was the place where Archander and Architeles, sons of Achæus, arrived from Phthiotis and became sons-in-law of Danaus. The Achæan name became attached to the population of Argos and Lacedæmon, although the Argives were privately called Danai, until the Dorians expelled the Achæans.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Achæans were descended through Achæus and became a general name for the populations of Argos and Lacedæmon, though the Argives were also called Danai. Expelled by the Dorians, they under Tisamenus fought the Ionians, defeated them, and settled in Ægialus.

l: Tisamenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Tisamenus, son of Orestes, was king of the Achæans after the Dorians expelled them from Argos and Lacedæmon. He fell in the battle against the Ionians, was buried at Helice, and his remains were later moved by the Lacedæmonians to Sparta.

l: the battle between the Ionians and Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The battle began after the Ionians rejected the Achæans' proposal to become their colonists because they feared Tisamenus would rule both peoples. Tisamenus fell, the Achæans defeated the Ionians, and the Ionians fled to Helice before being allowed to leave under conditions.

l: the Ionian migration to Attica, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Ionians migrated to Attica after their conflict with the Achæans. The Athenians and their king Melanthus welcomed them, either in gratitude for Ion's service or because they feared the Dorians and valued the Ionians' strength.

l: the naming of Achaia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Description of Greece, Volume II / BOOK VII.--ACHAIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The country between Elis and Sicyonia was called Achaia in Pausanias's time because of its inhabitants. In earlier times it was called Ægialus, and its inhabitants were called Ægialians or, after Ion, Ionian Ægialians.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, notes
s: Ægialus is identified as the Greek word for sea-shore. The note compares this interpretation with the names Pomerania and Glamorganshire. The Iliad, book II, line 575, is cited in connection with the discussion.

l: Ægialus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, notes
s: Ægialus is identified as the Greek word for sea-shore. Its meaning is compared with the names Pomerania and Glamorganshire.

l: the sea-shore, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, notes
s: Sea-shore is given as the meaning of the Greek word Ægialus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Medon and Nileus, sons of Codrus, disputed the Athenian kingship, but the oracle at Delphi assigned it to Medon, so Nileus and other sons of Codrus led a colony to Asia Minor. The expedition included Ionians, Thebans, Minyæ, Phocians, Abantes, and others, who founded or occupied several coastal cities, including Miletus, Ephesus, Priene, and Myus. Nileus and his forces conquered Miletus, killing its male inhabitants except those who escaped and marrying their women and daughters. Androclus drove the Leleges and Lydians from Ephesus, while the inhabitants of Myus later abandoned their city after the Mæander formed a marsh that bred immense numbers of mosquitoes.

l: Medon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Medon quarreled with his brother Nileus over who should rule the Athenians. Although he was lame in one foot, the Pythian Priestess at Delphi assigned the kingdom to him.

l: Nileus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Nileus refused to submit to Medon because Medon was lame in one foot. After the oracle assigned the kingdom to Medon, Nileus led a contingent to Asia Minor and later conquered Miletus.

l: Codrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Codrus was the father of Medon, Nileus, Androclus, and other sons who took part in colonies or expeditions. His sons were described as having Messenian ancestry through Codrus and Melanthus and Athenian ancestry on their mother's side.

l: Miletus (the Cretan leader), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Miletus led an expedition of Cretans to the country formerly called Anactoria, after which the town and country took the name Miletus. He and his force had fled Crete from Minos, the son of Europa.

l: Androclus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Androclus, the son of Codrus, was appointed king of the Ionians who sailed to Ephesus. He drove the Leleges and Lydians from the upper part of the city, took Samos from the Samians, and later assisted Priene against the Carians, dying in that battle.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Athenians were involved in the dispute between Medon and Nileus over their kingship. Philogenes and Damon, sons of Euctemon, gave ships to the Phocians and led them to the colony.

l: Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Ionians formed the largest part of the contingent led by Nileus and the other sons of Codrus. They settled several cities in Asia Minor, conquered Miletus, and inhabited Myus and Priene.

l: Cretans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Cretans under Miletus came to the country near Miletus while it was still called Anactoria. The Carians who had settled there earlier admitted them to a joint share of the territory.

l: Carians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Carians had settled near Miletus before the arrival of Miletus and the Cretans and shared the country with them. They were later driven from Miletus, Myus, and Priene by the Ionians or their associated settlers.

l: the sons of Codrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The sons of Codrus disputed or received leadership after Medon was assigned the Athenian kingdom. Nileus and the other sons were sent to found a colony, while Androclus led the Ionians who sailed to Ephesus and Cyaretus colonized Myus.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Athens was the starting point for the expedition led by the sons of Codrus. The Ionians sailed from Athens one generation before the account describes their settlement in Asia Minor.

l: Asia Minor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The sons of Codrus and their contingent crossed to Asia Minor, where different detachments settled different maritime towns. Miletus, Ephesus, Priene, and Myus are among the places associated with this settlement.

l: Miletus (city), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Miletus was formerly called Anactoria for two generations, during the reigns of Anax the Autochthon and his son Asterius. Nileus and the Ionians conquered it, killed its male inhabitants except those who escaped, and married their wives and daughters.

l: Ephesus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Ephesus was associated with Ephesus, thought to be the son of the river Cayster, and was inhabited by Leleges and most of the Lydians before the Ionian settlement. Androclus drove the Leleges and Lydians from the upper city, while those living near the temple remained on peaceful terms with the Ionians.

l: Priene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Priene was colonized by Thebans and Ionians under Philotas and Æpytus, and the Carians were driven from it. It was later ravaged by Tabalus the Persian and by Hiero, one of its own citizens, before becoming an Ionian city.

l: Myus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Myus was colonized by Cyaretus, the son of Codrus, and the Ionians drove the Carians from it. Its inhabitants later abandoned the town for Miletus after the nearby bay became a mosquito-filled marsh, carrying away what they could and the statues of the gods; in the narrator's time, only a white-marble temple of Dionysus remained.

l: expedition of the Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The expedition of the Ionians was led by Nileus and the other sons of Codrus and included people from Athens, Thebes, Orchomenus, Phocis, and Eubœa. After reaching Asia Minor, its detachments went to different maritime towns, including Miletus, Ephesus, Priene, and Myus.

l: Ionian migration, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Ionian migration brought the sons of Codrus and various Greek peoples to Asia Minor. The settlers conquered or occupied coastal cities and were not all related to the Ionians by race, since the sons of Codrus were Messenian through their fathers' ancestry and Athenian through their mother's side.

l: conquest of Miletus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: During the conquest of Miletus, the Ionians killed all the male inhabitants except those who escaped from the captured city. They married the surviving women and daughters.

l: marsh formation at Myus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Mæander filled the mouth of the bay near Myus with mud, turning it into a marsh. The foul water bred mosquitoes in immense numbers and forced the inhabitants of Myus to leave for Miletus.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The worship of the Ephesian Artemis was older than the Ionian migration. Pindar said that the Amazons who fought Theseus and Athens built her temple, but the account rejects this and says that Coresus and Ephesus built it; Amazons had previously sacrificed there and sought refuge near the temple.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Colophonians regard the temple and oracle of Apollo at Claros as ancient, tracing their origins to Cretans under Rhacius and later to Manto, Mopsus, and Ionian settlers. Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Erythræ, Clazomenæ, and Phocæa are described through traditions of Greek migration, interaction with the Carians, and later changes under rulers such as Lysimachus and Alexander. The account also explains the depopulation of Colophon and Lebedus, the settlement of Ephesus, and the origins of the Ionian communities in Asia Minor.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Apollo received Manto and the other captives at Delphi after the Argives and Thersander took Thebes. He later sent them to form a colony, leading them toward Asia Minor and Claros.

l: temple of Apollo at Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Colophonians regard the temple of Apollo at Claros as most ancient.

l: oracle of Apollo at Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Colophonians regard the oracle of Apollo at Claros as most ancient.

l: Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Claros was reached by the Cretans under Rhacius and by the captives sent by Apollo to form a colony. The Cretans attacked the newcomers there and brought them before Rhacius.
