l: Carians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Carians possessed most of the country around Claros when the first Greeks arrived. They were also mixed with the Greeks at Teos and Erythræ, and Mopsus later drove them altogether from the territory associated with Colophon.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The first Greeks said to reach the country around Claros were Cretans under Rhacius. Greeks also settled or participated in the foundations of Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Erythræ, Clazomenæ, and Phocæa.

l: Cretans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Cretans were the first Greeks said to have reached the country around Claros, arriving in a large force under Rhacius. They attacked the colonists sent by Apollo and took them before Rhacius.

l: Rhacius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Rhacius led the Cretans to Claros while the Carians still held most of the country. After understanding Manto's identity and mission, he married her and made her companions fellow-settlers with him.

l: Manto, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Manto was among the captives taken to Apollo at Delphi after the capture of Thebes. At Claros, Rhacius learned from her who the captives were and why they had come, then married her.

l: Asia Minor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Asia Minor was reached by the people whom Apollo sent to form a colony. Cretans, Ionians, and other Greek groups later settled or established cities there.

l: Mopsus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Mopsus, the son of Rhacius and Manto, drove out all the Carians altogether.

l: Colophonian Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Colophonian Greeks became fellow-citizens on equal terms with the Ionians. They were the only colonists at Ephesus who fought against Lysimachus and the Macedonians.

l: Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Ionians became fellow-citizens with the Colophonian Greeks on mutual and equal terms. They settled at places including Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Erythræ, Clazomenæ, and Phocæa, and later required Phocæa to accept kings descended from Codrus before admitting it to the Pan-Ionic confederacy.

l: Colophon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Colophon was associated with Cretan, Ionian, and other Greek settlement after Mopsus drove out the Carians. It was later dispeopled by Lysimachus, and the tombs of its people who fell in battle with those from Smyrna stood on the road to Claros.

l: Codrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Codrus was the ancestor of leaders and settlers connected with the Ionian cities. His descendants Damasichthon and Promethus ruled the Ionians, while Apœcus, Cleopus, Andræmon, Damasus, and Naoclus were also described as descendants of Codrus or associated with his line.

l: Lysimachus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Lysimachus dispeopled Colophon and Lebedus in order to increase the population of Ephesus. The colonists of Colophon fought against him and the Macedonians at Ephesus.

l: Ephesus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Ephesus received inhabitants from Colophon and Lebedus after Lysimachus dispeopled those cities. The colonists from Colophon were the only colonists there who fought against Lysimachus and the Macedonians.

l: Lebedus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Lebedus was dispeopled by Lysimachus to add to the population of Ephesus. It had been inhabited by the Carians before Andræmon and the Ionians drove them out, and it was noted for its numerous agreeable warm baths near the sea.

l: Teos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Teos was colonized by Minyæ from Orchomenus who came with Athamas, and Carians were mixed with the Greeks there. The Ionians were led to Teos by Apœcus, and later settlers from Attica and Bœotia were hospitably received.

l: Apœcus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Apœcus, a great-great-grandson of Melanthus, led the Ionians to Teos. He and the people of Teos hospitably received later settlers from Attica and Bœotia.

l: Erythræi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Erythræi said that they originally came from Crete with Erythrus, the founder of their city. They also described the later presence of Lycians, Carians, Pamphylians, and Greeks at Erythræ.

l: Erythræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Erythræ was founded by Erythrus, son of Rhadamanthys, and was initially associated with settlers from Crete. Lycians, Carians, Pamphylians, and other Greeks later occupied it, and Cleopus gathered people from the Ionian towns into a colony there.

l: Clazomenæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Clazomenæ had no city before the Ionians came to Asia Minor. Its settlers first built a city under Mount Ida, later returned to Ionia, and then occupied the territory of Clazomenæ; they subsequently moved to the opposite island because of the Persians, and Alexander later connected the island to the mainland by an embankment.

l: Phocæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Phocæa had no city before the Ionians came to Asia Minor. Its people came from the country under Mount Parnassus with Philogenes and Damon, obtained territory by agreement with the people of Cyme, and accepted kings from the descendants of Codrus in order to join the Pan-Ionic confederacy.

l: colonization of Asia Minor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The colonization of Asia Minor involved Cretans under Rhacius, captives sent by Apollo, Ionians, and other Greek groups. It produced settlements and cities including Claros, Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Erythræ, Clazomenæ, and Phocæa.
